{{Short description|Mathematical function}}

'''Slepian functions''' are a class of spatio-spectrally concentrated functions<ref name="i772">{{cite journal | last=Slepian | first=David | title=Some comments on Fourier analysis, uncertainty and modeling | journal=SIAM Review | volume=25 | issue=3 | date=1983 | issn=0036-1445 | doi=10.1137/1025078 | pages=379–393 | url=http://epubs.siam.org/doi/10.1137/1025078 | access-date=2025-07-03| url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref name="s666">{{cite book | last=Simons | first=Frederik J. | title=Handbook of Geomathematics | chapter=Slepian Functions and Their Use in Signal Estimation and Spectral Analysis | publisher=Springer Berlin Heidelberg | publication-place=Berlin, Heidelberg | date=2010 | isbn=978-3-642-01545-8 | doi=10.1007/978-3-642-01546-5_30 | pages=891–923| arxiv=0909.5368 }}</ref> that form an [[orthogonal basis]] for bandlimited or spacelimited spaces.<ref name="e945">{{cite book | last=Daubechies | first=Ingrid | title=Ten Lectures on Wavelets | publisher=SIAM | publication-place=Philadelphia (Pa.) | date=1992-06-01 | isbn=0-89871-274-2 | page=}}</ref><ref name="i703">{{cite book | last=Flandrin | first=Patrick | title=Time-frequency/time Scale Analysis | publisher=Academic Press | publication-place=San Diego | date=1999 | isbn=978-0-12-259870-8 | page=}}</ref><ref name="h134">{{cite book | last1=Hogan | first1=Jeffrey A. | last2=Lakey | first2=Joseph D. | title=Duration and Bandwidth Limiting | publisher=Birkhäuser | publication-place=Boston | date=2011-12-11 | isbn=978-0-8176-8306-1 | page=}}</ref><ref name="k094">{{cite book | last1=Kennedy | first1=Rodney A. | last2=Sadeghi | first2=Parastoo | title=Hilbert Space Methods in Signal Processing | publisher=Cambridge University Press | publication-place=Cambridge | date=2013-03-07 | isbn=978-1-107-01003-1 | page=}}</ref> That is, they are concentrated in space or time while spectrally bandlimited, or concentrated in spectral band while space- or time-limited. They are widely used as basis functions for [[Approximation theory| constructive approximation]]<ref name="d219">{{cite book | last=Michel | first=Volker | title=Lectures on Constructive Approximation | chapter=Spherical Slepian Functions | series=Applied and Numerical Harmonic Analysis | publisher=Birkhäuser Boston | publication-place=Boston | date=2013 | isbn=978-0-8176-8402-0 | doi=10.1007/978-0-8176-8403-7_8 | chapter-url=https://link.springer.com/10.1007/978-0-8176-8403-7_8 | access-date=2025-06-25 | pages=239–245}}</ref> and in linear [[inverse problem]]s,<ref name="o600">{{cite journal | last1=Simons | first1=Frederik J. | last2=Dahlen | first2=F. A. | title=Spherical Slepian functions and the polar gap in geodesy | journal=Geophysical Journal International | volume=166 | issue=3 | date=2006 | doi=10.1111/j.1365-246X.2006.03065.x | doi-access=free | pages=1039–1061 | arxiv=math/0603271 | bibcode=2006GeoJI.166.1039S | url=https://academic.oup.com/gji/article-pdf/166/3/1039/6098905/166-3-1039.pdf | access-date=2025-06-25}}</ref><ref name="y879">{{cite journal | last1=Michel | first1=Volker | last2=Simons | first2=Frederik J | title=A general approach to regularizing inverse problems with regional data using Slepian wavelets | journal=Inverse Problems | volume=33 | issue=12 | date=2017-12-01 | issn=0266-5611 | doi=10.1088/1361-6420/aa9909 | doi-access=free | page=125016 | arxiv=1708.04462 | bibcode=2017InvPr..33l5016M }}</ref> and as [[apodization]] tapers or [[window function]]s<ref name="t988">{{cite journal | last=Harris | first=F.J. | title=On the use of windows for harmonic analysis with the discrete Fourier transform | journal=Proceedings of the IEEE | volume=66 | issue=1 | date=1978 | issn=0018-9219 | doi=10.1109/PROC.1978.10837 | pages=51–83 }}</ref> in quadratic problems<ref name="t962">{{cite book | last=Haykin | first=Simon S. | title=Advances in Spectrum Analysis and Array Processing | publisher=Prentice Hall | publication-place=Englewood, Cliffs, N.J | date=1991 | isbn=978-0-13-007444-7 | page=}}</ref> of [[spectral density estimation]].<ref name="o228">{{cite journal | last=Thomson | first=D.J. | title=Spectrum estimation and harmonic analysis | journal=Proceedings of the IEEE | volume=70 | issue=9 | date=1982 | issn=0018-9219 | doi=10.1109/PROC.1982.12433 | pages=1055–1096 }}</ref><ref name="w675">{{cite journal | last1=Dahlen | first1=F. A. | last2=Simons | first2=Frederik J. | title=Spectral estimation on a sphere in geophysics and cosmology | journal=Geophysical Journal International | volume=174 | issue=3 | date=2008 | doi=10.1111/j.1365-246X.2008.03854.x | doi-access=free | pages=774–807 | arxiv=0705.3083 | bibcode=2008GeoJI.174..774D | url=https://academic.oup.com/gji/article-pdf/174/3/774/5889898/174-3-774.pdf | access-date=2025-06-25}}</ref>

Slepian function constructions exist in discrete (regular<ref name="j530">{{cite journal | last=Slepian | first=D. | title=Prolate Spheroidal Wave Functions, Fourier Analysis, and Uncertainty-V: The Discrete Case | journal=Bell System Technical Journal | volume=57 | issue=5 | date=1978-05-06 | doi=10.1002/j.1538-7305.1978.tb02104.x | pages=1371–1430 | url=https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/6771595 | access-date=2025-07-03| url-access=subscription }}</ref> and irregular<ref name="q854">{{cite journal | last=Bronez | first=T.P. | title=Spectral estimation of irregularly sampled multidimensional processes by generalized prolate spheroidal sequences | journal=IEEE Transactions on Acoustics, Speech, and Signal Processing | volume=36 | issue=12 | date=1988 | doi=10.1109/29.9031 | pages=1862–1873 | url=https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/9031 | access-date=2025-07-03| url-access=subscription }}</ref>) and continuous<ref name="q757">{{cite journal | last1=Slepian | first1=D. | last2=Pollak | first2=H. ==General setting and operator formalism==

Without reference to any of these particularities,<ref name="j782">{{cite journal | last1=Simons | first1=Frederik J. | last2=Dahlen | first2=F. A. | last3=Wieczorek | first3=Mark A. | title=Spatiospectral Concentration on a Sphere | journal=SIAM Review | volume=48 | issue=3 | date=2006 | issn=0036-1445 | doi=10.1137/S0036144504445765 | doi-access=free | pages=504–536 | arxiv=math/0408424 | bibcode=2006SIAMR..48..504S | url=https://hal.science/hal-02458541/document | access-date=2025-06-25}}</ref> let <math>f</math> be a [[square-integrable function]] of physical space, and let <math>\mathcal{H}</math> represent Fourier transformation, such that <math>F=\mathcal{H}f</math> and <math>\mathcal{H}^{-1}F=f</math>.
Let the operators <math>\mathcal{R}</math> and <math>\mathcal{L}</math> project onto the space of spacelimited functions,
<math>\mathcal{S}_R</math>, and the space of bandlimited functions, <math>\mathcal{S}_L</math>, respectively, whereby <math>R</math> is an arbitrary nontrivial subregion of all of physical space, and <math>L</math> an arbitrary nontrivial subregion of spectral space. Thus, the operator <math>\mathcal{R}</math> acts to spacelimit, and the operator
<math>\mathcal{H}^{-1}\mathcal{L}\mathcal{H}</math> acts to bandlimit the function <math>f</math>.

Slepian's quadratic [[spectral concentration problem]] aims to maximize the concentration of spectral power to a target region <math>L</math>, for a function that is spatially limited to a target region  <math>R</math>. Conversely, Slepian's spatial concentration problem maximizes the spatial concentration to <math>R</math> of a function bandlimited to <math>L</math>. Using <math>\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle</math> for the inner product both in the space and the spectral domains, both problems are stated equivalently using [[Rayleigh quotient]]s in the form

<math>
\lambda=
\frac{\langle\mathcal{R}\mathcal{H}^{-1}\mathcal{L}\,F,
\mathcal{R}\mathcal{H}^{-1}\mathcal{L}\,F\,\rangle}
{\langle\mathcal{H}^{-1}\mathcal{L}\,F,
\mathcal{H}^{-1}\mathcal{L}\,F\,\rangle}=\frac{\langle\mathcal{L}\mathcal{H}\mathcal{R}f,
\mathcal{L}\mathcal{H}\mathcal{R}f\rangle} {\langle\mathcal{H}\mathcal{R}f, \mathcal{H}\mathcal{R}
f\rangle}=\mbox{maximum}
.
</math>

The equivalent spectral-domain and spatial-domain eigenvalue equations are

<math>(\mathcal{L}\mathcal{H}\mathcal{R}\mathcal{H}^{-1\!}\mathcal{L})(\mathcal{L}\,F\,)
=\lambda(\mathcal{L}\,F\,)
</math> and <math>
(\mathcal{R}\mathcal{H}^{-1\!}\mathcal{L}\mathcal{H}\mathcal{R})(\mathcal{R}f)=\lambda(\mathcal{R}f),</math>

given that <math>\mathcal{H}</math> and <math>\mathcal{H}^{-1}</math> are each others' [[Hermitian adjoint|adjoints]], and that
<math>\mathcal{R}</math> and <math>\mathcal{L}</math> are [[Self-adjoint operator|self-adjoint]] and [[Idempotence|idempotent]].

The Slepian functions are solutions to either of these types of equations with [[positive-definite kernel]]s, that is, they are bandlimited functions
<math>G=\mathcal{L}F</math>, concentrated to the spatial domain within <math>R</math>, or spacelimited functions of the form
<math>h=\mathcal{R}f</math>, concentrated to the spectral domain within <math>L</math>.

== Scalar Slepian functions in one dimension ==
[[File:Properties of the one-dimensional scalar Slepian functions.gif|thumb|(a) Slepian functions in the time domain. (b) Slepian functions in the frequency domain. Shown is the square of the absolute value of the Fourier transform of the Slepian functions shown in (a). (c) Concentration factors associated with the successive Slepian functions shown in (a). (d) Cumulative energy by summation the square of the Slepian functions shown in (a).]]
Let <math>g(t)</math> and its [[Fourier transform]] <math>G(\omega)</math> be strictly bandlimited in [[angular frequency]] between <math>[-W,W]</math>. Attempting to concentrate <math>g(t)</math> in the [[time domain]], to be contained within the time interval <math>[-T,T]</math>, amounts to maximizing

<math>
\lambda=\frac{\int_{-T}^{T}g^2(t)\,dt}{\int_{-\infty}^\infty g^2(t)\,dt}=\text{maximum}
,
</math>

which is equivalent to solving either, in the [[frequency domain]], the [[convolution]]al integral eigenvalue ([[Fredholm integral equation|Fredholm]]) equation

<math>\int_{-W}^{W}D_T(\omega,\omega')G(\omega')\,d\omega'=\lambda G(\omega),\qquad D_T(\omega,\omega')=\frac{\sin T(\omega-\omega')}{\pi(\omega-\omega')}, \qquad |\omega|\le W,</math>

or the time- or space-domain version

<math>\int_{-T}^{T}D_W(t,t')g(t')\,dt'=\lambda g(t),\qquad D_W(t,t')=\frac{\sin W(t-t')}{\pi(t-t')}=
(2\pi)^{-1}\int_{-W}^{W}e^{i\omega(t-t')}d\omega,
\qquad t \in \mathbb{R}.</math>

Either of these can be transformed and rescaled to the dimensionless

<math>\int_{-1}^{1}D(x,x')g(x')\,dx'=\lambda g(x),\qquad D(x,x')=\frac{\sin TW(x-x')}{\pi(x-x')}.</math>

The trace of the [[Positive-definite kernel|positive definite kernel]] is the sum of the infinite number of real and positive eigenvalues,

<math>N=\sum_{\alpha=1}^\infty \lambda_\alpha=\int_{-1}^{1}D(x,x')\,dx=\frac{2TW}{\pi},</math>

that is, the area of the concentration domain in time-frequency space (a time-bandwidth product).

One-dimensional scalar Slepian functions or tapers<ref name="q951">{{cite book | last=Press | first=William H. | title=Numerical Recipes 3rd Edition | publisher=Cambridge University Press | publication-place=Cambridge | date=2007-09-06 | isbn=978-0-521-88068-8 | page=}}</ref> are the workhorse of the [[David J. Thomson|Thomson]] [[multitaper]] method of [[spectral density estimation]].

== Scalar Slepian functions in two Cartesian dimensions ==
[[File:Slepian 2D Cartesian Cat Duck.png|thumb|upright=1.35|Slepian functions concentrated to a cat-like spatial (top row; rank <math>\alpha</math> and concentration eigenvalue <math>\lambda</math>) and a duck-like spectral domain (bottom row; shown is the square of the absolute value of the Fourier transform of the functions shown in the top row).]]
We use <math>g(\mathbf{x})</math> and its Fourier transform <math>G(\mathbf{k})</math> to denote a function that is strictly bandlimited to <math>\mathcal{K}</math>, an arbitrary subregion of the spectral space of spatial wave vectors.<ref name="g655">{{cite journal | last1=Simons | first1=Frederik J. | last2=Wang | first2=Dong V. | title=Spatiospectral concentration in the Cartesian plane | journal=GEM - International Journal on Geomathematics | volume=2 | issue=1 | date=2011 | issn=1869-2672 | doi=10.1007/s13137-011-0016-z | doi-access=free | pages=1–36 | arxiv=1007.5226 | bibcode=2011IJGm....2....1S }}</ref>
Seeking to concentrate <math>g(\mathbf{x})</math> into a finite spatial region <math>R\in\mathbb{R}^2</math>,
of area <math>A</math>, we must find the unknown functions for which

<math>
\lambda=\frac{\int_{R}g^2(\mathbf{x})\,d\mathbf{x}}
{\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} g^2(\mathbf{x})\,d\mathbf{x}}=\mbox{maximum}.
</math>

Maximizing this Rayleigh quotient requires solving the Fredholm integral equation

<math>
\int_\mathcal{K}D_R(\mathbf{k},\mathbf{k}')\,G(\mathbf{k}')\,d\mathbf{k}'
=\lambda G(\mathbf{k})
,
\qquad
D_R(\mathbf{k},\mathbf{k}')=(2\pi)^{-2}
\int_R e^{i(\mathbf{k}'-\mathbf{k})\cdot\mathbf{x}}\,d\mathbf{x}
,\qquad \mathbf{k}\in\mathcal{K}.
</math>

The corresponding problem in the spatial domain is

<math>
\int_R\! D_\mathcal{K}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{x}')\,g(\mathbf{x}')\,d\mathbf{x}'
=\lambda g(\mathbf{x}),\qquad
D_\mathcal{K}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{x}')=(2\pi)^{-2}
\int_\mathcal{K} e^{i\mathbf{k}\cdot(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{x}')}\,d\mathbf{k},\qquad\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^2.
</math>

Concentration to the disk-shaped spectral band
<math>\mathcal{K}=\{\mathbf{k}:\|\mathbf{k}\|\le K\}</math> allows us to rewrite the spatial kernel as

<math>
D_\mathcal{K}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{x}')=\frac{KJ_1(K\|\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{x}'\|)}{2\pi\|\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{x}'\|},
</math>

with <math>J_1</math> a [[Bessel function | Bessel function of the first kind]], from which we may derive that

<math>N=\sum_{\alpha=1}^\infty \lambda_\alpha=\int_RD_\mathcal{K}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{x})\,d\mathbf{x}=K^2\frac{A}{4\pi},</math>

in other words, again the area of the concentration domain in space-frequency space (a space-bandwidth product).

== Scalar Slepian functions on the surface of a sphere==
[[File:Spherical Slepian functions for the polar cap.gif|thumb|upright=1.35|Spherical Slepian functions of spherical-harmonic bandwidth 18, and of spherical-harmonic order 0 (that is, only made of zonal spherical harmonics), either very well (top row) or very poorly (bottom row) concentrated, as indicated by the concentration ratio <math>\lambda</math> to the North-polar cap of opening angle 40<math>^\circ</math>.]]
We denote <math>g(\mathbf{\hat{r}})</math> a function on the [[unit sphere]] <math>\Omega</math> and its [[spherical harmonic]] transform coefficient <math>g_{lm}</math> at the degree <math>l</math>
and order <math>m</math>, respectively,<ref name="j782" /> and we consider bandlimitation to spherical harmonic degree <math>L</math>, that is, <math>g\in \mathcal{S}_L</math>. Maximizing the quadratic energy ratio within the spatial subdomain <math>R\subset \Omega</math> via

<math>
\lambda=
\frac{\int_R g^2(\mathbf{\hat{r}})\,d\Omega}
{\int_{\Omega}g^2(\mathbf{\hat{r}})\,d\Omega}
=\mbox{maximum}
</math>

amounts in the spectral domain to solving the algebraic eigenvalue equation

<math>\sum_{l'=0}^L\sum_{m'=-l'}^{l'}D_{lm,l'm'}g_{l'm'}=\lambda g_{lm},\qquad D_{lm,l'm'}=\int_R Y_{lm}(\mathbf{\hat{r}})Y_{l'm'}(\mathbf{\hat{r}})\,d\Omega</math>,

with <math>Y_{lm}</math> the spherical harmonic at  degree <math>l</math> and order <math>m</math>. The equivalent spatial-domain equation,
<math>\int_R D(\mathbf{\hat{r}},\mathbf{\hat{r}}')g(\mathbf{\hat{r}})\,d\Omega
= \lambda g(\mathbf{\hat{r}}),\qquad D(\mathbf{\hat{r}},\mathbf{\hat{r}}') =
\sum_{l=0}^L\sum_{m=-l}^{l}Y_{lm}(\mathbf{\hat{r}})Y_{lm}(\mathbf{\hat{r}}')
=\sum_{l=0}^L
\left(\frac{2l+1}{4\pi}\right)
P_l(\mathbf{\hat{r}}\cdot\mathbf{\hat{r}}'),</math>
is a homogeneous [[Fredholm integral equation]] of the second kind, with a finite-rank, symmetric, separable kernel.

The last equality is a consequence of the [[Spherical harmonics#Addition theorem|spherical harmonic addition theorem]] which involves <math>P_l</math>, the [[Legendre polynomial]]. The trace of this kernel is given by

<math>N=\sum_{\alpha=1}^{(L+1)^2}\lambda_\alpha=\int_R
D(\mathbf{\hat{r}},\mathbf{\hat{r}})\,d\Omega=
\sum_{l=0}^L\sum_{m=-l}^{l}D_{lm,lm}
=(L+1)^2\frac{A}{4\pi},</math>

that is, once again a space-bandwidth product, of the dimension of <math> \mathcal{S}_L</math> and the fractional area of <math>R</math> on the unit sphere <math>\Omega</math>, namely <math>A/(4\pi)</math>.
